title: 10 Database Concepts You Can't Skip in System Design Interviews
summary: Ten database concepts that system design interviews keep returning to, ordered from foundational to advanced: Transactions, ACID, Indexing, Isolation Levels, Locking, MVCC, Connection Pooling, Replication, Partitioning and Sharding. Each gets a worked example, its trade-offs and the interview takeaway.

chapters.title: Database Concepts for System Design Interviews
points: Cover promise: ten database concepts that decide how a system survives scale, failure and concurrency
The ten, foundational to advanced: Transactions, ACID, Indexing, Isolation Levels, Locking, MVCC, Connection Pooling, Replication, Partitioning, Sharding
Every concept follows one pattern: what it is, why it exists, used for, how it works, benefits, things to consider, interview takeaway
Who it is for: backend engineers preparing for system design rounds

chapters.title: Transactions
points: What it is: a group of reads and writes the database treats as one all-or-nothing unit of work
Why it exists: a crash or error halfway through a multi-step change would leave data half-updated and inconsistent
Used for: money transfers, order placement, inventory decrement plus order insert, any change spanning several rows or tables

How it works: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 100 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT; if the second UPDATE fails, ROLLBACK restores both balances (account 1: 500, account 2: 200)
Benefits: no partial writes, simple error handling (rollback on any failure), safe retries, a clear boundary for a business operation
Things to consider: long transactions hold locks and bloat the log, a transaction spans one database only (cross-service work needs sagas or 2PC), and keep external calls like HTTP out of it
Interview takeaway: keep transactions short and scoped to one database, and name the saga pattern when the work spans services

chapters.title: ACID
points: What it is: four guarantees a transactional database gives: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
Why it exists: without them, concurrency and crashes silently corrupt data and every app would reimplement safety by hand
Used for: choosing between relational stores (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) and weaker NoSQL stores for payments, ledgers and bookings

How it works: Atomicity via undo log, Consistency via constraints, Isolation via locks or MVCC, Durability via a write-ahead log fsynced at COMMIT; transferring 100 from an account holding 50 hits CHECK (bal >= 0), the whole transaction aborts and no money moves
Benefits: data stays correct under crashes and concurrency, invariants live in the database instead of app code, committed data survives power loss
Things to consider: ACID costs latency (an fsync per commit), Consistency in ACID is not the Consistency in CAP, and many NoSQL stores trade it for availability and scale
Interview takeaway: say what each letter means and which mechanism implements it (undo log, constraints, locks/MVCC, WAL)

chapters.title: Indexing
points: What it is: a separate sorted structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table
Why it exists: a full scan of 10M rows is O(n), while a B-tree lookup is O(log n), about 3-4 page reads
Used for: WHERE filters, JOIN keys, ORDER BY and range queries, and enforcing UNIQUE

How it works: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_created ON orders(user_id, created_at); SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10 walks the tree to user 42 and reads the 10 newest entries already sorted
Benefits: reads drop from seconds to milliseconds, sorting comes free, a covering index avoids touching the table at all

Things to consider: every index slows INSERT/UPDATE and uses disk, column order matters (leftmost prefix rule), low-cardinality columns gain little, and WHERE LOWER(email) = ... bypasses a plain index
Interview takeaway: index for your query patterns, put equality columns before range columns, and always mention the write-cost trade-off

chapters.title: Isolation Levels
points: What it is: a setting that controls how much concurrent transactions can see of each other's uncommitted or newer changes
Why it exists: full isolation (Serializable) is slow, so databases let you trade correctness for throughput
Used for: tuning concurrency per workload: reports tolerate weaker levels while money movement needs stronger ones

How it works: Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads, Read Committed blocks them, Repeatable Read blocks non-repeatable reads, Serializable also blocks phantoms and write skew; two on-call doctors both check 'at least 2 on call' and both go off call, which commits under Repeatable Read but aborts one under Serializable
Benefits: a tunable dial between speed and correctness, weaker levels give higher throughput and fewer aborts, Serializable gives the strongest guarantee
Things to consider: defaults differ (PostgreSQL Read Committed, MySQL InnoDB Repeatable Read), higher levels raise aborts, and the app must retry on serialization failure
Interview takeaway: name the anomalies (dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, write skew) and which level prevents each; Read Committed is the usual default

chapters.title: Locking
points: What it is: a mechanism where a transaction reserves a row or table so others cannot change it at the same time
Why it exists: two writers updating the same row concurrently cause lost updates, so access must be serialized
Used for: protecting counters, stock levels, seat bookings and balances from concurrent writes

How it works: pessimistic: SELECT stock FROM items WHERE id = 7 FOR UPDATE; blocks other writers until COMMIT; optimistic: UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1, version = 4 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 3; zero rows updated means retry
Benefits: prevents lost updates, pessimistic locking is simple and certain under high contention, optimistic locking holds no locks and scales under low contention
Things to consider: deadlocks (A waits on B, B on A) so lock rows in a consistent order, long locks hurt throughput, and optimistic retries waste work on conflict
Interview takeaway: pick pessimistic for hot rows with high contention and optimistic (version column) for rare conflicts; mention deadlock avoidance via lock ordering

chapters.title: MVCC
points: What it is: Multi-Version Concurrency Control keeps several versions of a row so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers
Why it exists: plain locking makes readers wait for writers, which cripples throughput on read-heavy workloads
Used for: PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB and Oracle to deliver snapshot reads under Read Committed and Repeatable Read

How it works: in PostgreSQL each row version carries xmin (creating txn) and xmax (deleting txn); txn 100 reads balance 500 while txn 101 updates it to 400, and txn 100 still sees 500 until it ends, with nobody waiting
Benefits: readers don't block writers and writers don't block readers, consistent snapshots, high read concurrency
Things to consider: old versions pile up as dead tuples so PostgreSQL needs VACUUM, long-running transactions block cleanup and cause bloat, and writers on the same row still conflict
Interview takeaway: say 'readers don't block writers and writers don't block readers', and tie bloat and VACUUM to long transactions

chapters.title: Connection Pooling
points: What it is: a cache of open database connections that application threads borrow and return, instead of opening a new one per request
Why it exists: opening a connection costs a TCP handshake, TLS and authentication (tens of ms), and each PostgreSQL connection is a process using several MB of memory
Used for: web backends with many concurrent requests, serverless functions, and protecting the database from connection storms

How it works: pool size 20 with 200 concurrent requests means 20 run at once and 180 wait in the queue, each connection returning to the pool after its query; PgBouncer in transaction mode multiplexes thousands of clients onto about 50 server connections
Benefits: lower latency per request, a hard cap on database load, reuse of prepared statements and sessions

Things to consider: a pool too big thrashes the database while one too small queues requests, leaked connections drain the pool, and transaction-mode pooling breaks session state such as SET and advisory locks
Interview takeaway: size the pool to the database (roughly cores x 2 plus spindles), not to the app thread count, and put PgBouncer in front when many app instances connect

chapters.title: Replication
points: What it is: keeping copies of the same data on multiple servers, with one primary taking writes and replicas following it
Why it exists: one server is a single point of failure and a read bottleneck
Used for: high availability, read scaling, geographic proximity, and offline analytics or backups

How it works: the primary writes changes to its WAL and ships them to replicas, where async returns the commit before the replica has it and sync waits for at least one replica; with a 2 second lag a user's new comment is missing on the next page load, fixed by reading from the primary right after a write
Benefits: failover in seconds when a primary dies, read throughput scales by adding replicas, data survives disk or zone loss
Things to consider: async replication can lose the last writes on failover, replica lag gives stale reads, sync replication adds write latency, and multi-leader setups need conflict resolution
Interview takeaway: state the sync versus async trade-off (durability against latency) and handle stale reads with read-your-writes routing

chapters.title: Partitioning
points: What it is: splitting one large table into smaller pieces (partitions) inside a single database server
Why it exists: huge tables make scans, index maintenance, vacuuming and deletes slow
Used for: time-series and log tables, archiving old data, and speeding up queries that touch one slice

How it works: PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) with monthly partitions means a query for March reads only orders_2026_03 (partition pruning), and dropping January is a DROP TABLE instead of a slow DELETE of 50M rows
Benefits: faster queries via pruning, smaller indexes per partition, cheap bulk deletes, easier maintenance
Things to consider: a query without the partition key scans all partitions, a bad key creates skew (one hot partition), and partitioning does not add servers
Interview takeaway: partitioning is within one node while sharding spans many nodes; pick range for time data and hash for even spread

chapters.title: Sharding
points: What it is: horizontally splitting data across multiple database servers, each shard holding a subset of rows
Why it exists: one machine eventually runs out of write throughput, storage or memory, and vertical scaling hits a ceiling
Used for: very large datasets and write-heavy systems at scale (users, messages, orders)

How it works: shard = hash(user_id) % 4 routes user 1042 to shard 2, with a router or the app computing the shard and sending the query there; consistent hashing lets you add shards while moving only about 1/N of the keys
Benefits: write and storage capacity scale almost linearly with shards, a failure is limited to one shard's users, shards can sit near their users
Things to consider: cross-shard joins and transactions are costly, resharding is painful, hot keys (a celebrity user) overload one shard, and the shard key is very hard to change later
Interview takeaway: shard last, after indexing, caching, replication and partitioning; choose a key with high cardinality and even load, and say how you would reshard

chapters.title: Cheatsheet: Database Concepts
points: Transactions: all-or-nothing unit of work; BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK; keep short
ACID: Atomicity (undo log), Consistency (constraints), Isolation (locks/MVCC), Durability (WAL)
Indexing: B-tree gives O(log n); leftmost prefix rule; costs writes and space
Isolation levels: Read Uncommitted < Read Committed < Repeatable Read < Serializable; anomalies are dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, write skew
Locking: pessimistic FOR UPDATE for hot rows, optimistic version column for rare conflicts; order locks to avoid deadlock
MVCC: row versions and snapshots; readers don't block writers; VACUUM cleans dead tuples
Connection pooling: reuse connections, cap load; size to the database, use PgBouncer

Replication copies data for availability and reads (watch lag); partitioning splits a table inside one server; sharding splits data across servers; scale in the order: index, cache, replicate, partition, shard
